title: Giving as practice
hookLine: the first perfection lived: give something daily this week
last: CIRCLE THE HOLY, KEEPING IT ON YOUR RIGHT.

lines: RICE INTO A BOWL AT DAWN.
NO THANK YOU, AND NO FAVOR.
cards: A bowl of rice is passed from hand to hand at dawn. A monk walks barefoot down a street, someone kneels and spoons food into his bowl, and the monk says nothing and walks on. Neither one says thank you.
That isn't rudeness. The giver isn't doing the monk a favor, and the monk isn't doing the giver one either.

After a week walking to the places of the Buddha's life, the path turns inward, to the perfections, the qualities Buddhists say a person grows on the way to awakening. The list begins with the simplest thing in that bowl.

teach.b: First, the list. Theravada Buddhists keep one list of perfections and Mahayana Buddhists keep another, differing in length and wording. But both begin in the same place: giving, dana.
Before anything else on either list, the open hand. Second, the Buddha's own claim. In a short collection called the Itivuttaka, he says something startling.
If people knew, as he knows, the fruit of giving and sharing, they would not eat without giving first.
Even their last bite, their last mouthful, they would not eat without sharing, if there were someone to share it with. Not the leftovers: the last mouthful. Third, two kinds of gift.
In the same collection, the Buddha names the gift of material things and the gift of the teaching. Bread is a gift.
So is a true word at the right time. Neither needs to be large. Fourth, why it's a practice and not just a kind act.

A verse of the Dhammapada, in Max Muller's old translation, puts it this way: "Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!"
Liberality is the old word for generosity, and here it's a medicine for grasping, including one's own. So giving, to monks, neighbors, strangers, isn't only to help, though it helps.
It's a way to practice letting go, one small thing at a time. That's why nobody needs to say thank you at the bowl. The giving was the practice.

how: Buddhists practice dana by offering food to monks and nuns, supporting temples, and giving to people in need, and in Theravada countries the morning alms round is a daily chance to give.

o: giving only to monks, never to strangers
giving away all you own to become a monk
giving to loosen your own grip, not only to help

games.q: giving as practice: tap the pairs.
p: still worth sharing, the Buddha says

s: the Theravada and Mahayana lists of perfections are identical
they differ in length and wording, but both begin with giving.
the Buddha says the teaching itself can be a gift
the Itivuttaka names two gifts: material things and the teaching.
giving only counts when it is something large
the Buddha's bar is even the last mouthful. the size is not the point.

games.q: you have one last bite of food. someone beside you has none. by the Buddha's words in the Itivuttaka, what would a person who knew the fruit of giving do?
o: eat it; it's the last one.
games.why: share it. he says that if people knew the fruit of giving, they would not eat even their last mouthful without sharing it, if someone were there to receive.

practice: Sit and breathe, and bring to mind one small thing you could give: a coin, a meal, an hour, a book you've finished, a true word to someone who needs it. Picture handing it over, and notice the hand opening. Rest in that open hand.

wordCard.voice: Giving as practice. Dana, the first of the perfections in both Theravada and Mahayana lists: giving not only to help, but to train the heart to let go. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit dana: giving, generosity, the first of the perfections.

carryVoice: Your line: the first perfection. It starts with an open hand. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.q: Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!
